b: About The Care Leaders From care leaver to care leader The Care Leaders is a children’s social care consultancy founded in 2017 by Luke Rodgers BEM. We bring lived experience of care and professional experience of changing services into the same room, so the people a service is for help shape it. Start a conversation See our work Our founder Luke Rodgers BEM Luke went into care at 10. At 15 he was living in a bed and breakfast, and at 18 in a caravan. He gave his first keynote at 19, to a room of professionals, and has spent his career since then inside children’s services: as a consultant, a trainer, a board member and a national engagement lead. He founded The Care Leaders in 2017 and the Care Leavers National Movement. He was awarded the British Empire Medal in 2018 for his commitment to children and families, and held a Knowledge Equity Fellowship at Saïd Business School, University of Oxford. He was a non-executive director of The Staff College sat on the advisory board of the Rees Centre at the University of Oxford and the Mockingbird programme board at The Fostering Network, and was a Young Person’s Ambassador for the National Fostering Agency. In 2026 he led the national engagement on the Department for Education’s rewrite of the Fostering Services National Minimum Standards. Book Luke to speak How we work Lived experience of care on its own is a story. Professional experience on its own is a method. We put the two together. 1 Lived experience People who grew up in care, left it and built lives and careers afterwards, including our founder and the care-experienced leaders we work with. 2 Professional experience Consultants who have run, redesigned and inspected children’s services, trained workforces and led national work with the Department for Education. 3 Co-production Children, families and staff shape every project, so what we leave behind is owned by the people who will use it. What we stand for Put family first. Every child deserves people who stay. Think big, deliver detail. Ambitious for services, meticulous about the work. Turn stories into strategy. Lived experience becomes plans, products and practice. Talk straight. We say what we see, kindly and clearly. Leave legacies. Everything we build is handed over to carry on without us. b: Accessibility Accessibility statement Last updated October 2026 Our aim We want everyone to be able to use thecareleaders.com, including people who use a screen reader, a keyboard, magnification or voice control. We build the site to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA. What we’ve done Text and buttons meet the contrast levels in WCAG 2.2 AA. Every page works with a keyboard and shows where you are with a visible focus outline. Buttons and links are large enough to tap. Text can be enlarged to 200% without losing content, and the layout works on phones. Images that carry meaning have text descriptions, and videos only load when you choose to play them. What we know still needs work Some brochures and reports you can download are PDFs designed for print, and may not work well with a screen reader. Some case studies show photos of documents and slides, and the words in those images aren’t always repeated on the page. If you need any of this in another format, ask us and we’ll send it. h1: Every behaviour is a message.

b: Understanding care Every behaviour is a message. For school staff, residential workers and foster carers who support children in care and children who need the most support. Your staff learn to read what a behaviour is telling them, stay calm through the hardest five minutes, put things right afterwards and write it up fairly. Fewer moments turn into incidents, and children keep the adults who help them settle. The schools version follows the DfE guidance on restrictive interventions in force from April 2026. t: Care Not Custody training
h1: A broken window is not a crime scene.
d: Joint training for children’s homes, police and youth justice teams to put the national protocol on reducing criminalisation into daily practice.
h: What changes · Session by session · Choose how you run it · Questions commissioners ask · Often booked with · Talk to us about Care Not Custody
b: NVR and relationships A broken window is not a crime scene. For children’s home staff, police officers and youth justice teams who deal with incidents involving children in care. Together, in one room, you put the DfE’s 2018 national protocol on reducing unnecessary criminalisation into everyday decisions. Things a reasonable parent would sort out at home get sorted out at home, serious harm still gets a police response, and children don’t pick up a record for being in care. Length 6 hours face to face, usually 10am to 4pm. 2 hours live online How Face to face or live online Group Up to 60 people For Children’s homes, police and youth justice teams Add to shortlist On your shortlist Ask about this course View your shortlist The problem it solves In a children’s home, a slammed door, a broken window or a push during an argument can end in a 999 call, a night in custody and a record that follows the child into adult life. In most families the same thing would be dealt with by a parent. The DfE’s national protocol (2018) asks one question of every response: “would this be good enough for my child?” Without a shared local agreement, the staff member on a late shift and the officer who turns up are left to answer it alone. This day starts from the child’s side of one evening like that, gives you the protocol and the thinking behind it, and ends with the decision guide and scripts your staff use on the next shift. Helps with Behaviour, incidents and restraint What changes For your staff For children What they learn Who it is for Ask “would I have called the police if this were my own child?” before picking up the phone, and record why they did or did not. Use the protocol’s three levels: deal with minor incidents in the home, decide carefully about police for less serious ones, and call straight away when there is a risk of serious harm. Calm things down first, delay the response until everyone is calm, and use a restorative conversation that still holds the child to account. Ask whether a child is being criminally exploited before treating them as an offender. Work with officers as partners, using options short of arrest and charge when police are involved. t: From Case Note to Letter training
h1: Write it to the child.
d: Training for social care staff on writing case notes, reports and life story pieces to the child. Bring a real piece and rewrite it in the room.
h: What changes · Session by session · Choose how you run it · Questions commissioners ask · Often booked with · Talk to us about From Case Note to Letter
b: Words that matter Write it to the child. For social workers, residential key workers, personal advisers and IROs who write about children in care. People learn to write case notes, review records and life story pieces to the child, keeping the facts and analysis a record needs while making it something the child could read at 8 or at 40. Everyone brings a real piece of their own writing and leaves with it rewritten. Length 6 hours face to face, usually 10am to 4pm. 2 hours live online How Face to face or live online Group Up to 60 people For Social workers, residential staff, personal advisers and IROs Add to shortlist On your shortlist Ask about this course View your shortlist The problem it solves Under the Care Planning, Placement and Case Review (England) Regulations 2010, a child’s case record is kept until their 75th birthday, and care-experienced adults can ask to read it, often to understand their own story. What they usually find is written for the organisation: risk, process and jargon. UCL’s MIRRA research with care-experienced adults found that records mainly serve services, and that children’s voices and feelings are often missing or misrepresented. This workshop starts where they do, reading a file from the child’s side. Then it gives you the thinking behind writing to the child and spends most of the time on your own writing. Helps with Recording and the words we use What changes For your staff For children What they learn Who it is for Write case notes and reports addressed to the child, in words they would understand, without losing facts or analysis. Separate what they saw, what was said and what they think, so a reader can tell fact from opinion. Explain decisions in the record, including the child’s view and the reasons when the decision went another way. Write about hard events truthfully, without blame or labels. Use shared team templates and prompts, so the change holds when staff move on. Records and letters they can read and recognise themselves in. Knowing why decisions about their lives were made, and that their view was written down. Finding the hard parts of their history written honestly and kindly. Client Darlington Borough Council, Darlington Virtual School When April 2025 to July 2026 Who took part Designated teachers from schools across Darlington Our role Co-design, programme design, resources and delivery 3 face-to-face days across the school year, with online sessions between 10 months one school year: learn in person, apply in school, reflect online 30 designated teachers trained On this page The starting point What we heard What we did How we worked What changed Start a conversation The starting point Every school must have a designated teacher for children in care. It is a statutory role, but the training and support rarely match its weight.
